text: Subscribe to skip adsAdvertisementPaleontologyHow Prehistoric People Survived After One of the Worst Volcanic Eruptions in HistoryIt’s a story of human resilienceJCBy Jake Currie3:00 PM CDT on October 15, 2026Add Nautilus to GoogleAround 5,250 BCE a series of volcanic activity rocked Japan’s southernmost island, Kyushu. Known as the Kikai-Akahoya eruption, the blast was enormous, notching a seven on the Volcanic Explosivity Index (which only goes up to eight), and causing waves of destruction that ravaged the greater archipelago.Powered By 10 ShareNextStay“This eruption must have been devastating, exploding out of the seabed with little warning,” Lund University archaeologist Peter Jordan explained in a statement. “It battered the Japanese islands with powerful earthquakes and enormous tsunamis, and then blanketed the landscape with meters of volcanic ash.” Read more: “A Blow‑by‑Blow Account of What Would Happen If the Yellowstone Supervolcano Erupted Now”Already have an account?Log inRead without limitsFinish this story and enjoy unlimited, ad-free access to Nautilus.
